prompt: Single gene with two alleles: B (dominant, colored flower) and b (recessive, white flower). Complete dominance: any genotype with at least one B shows colored flowers; only bb shows white flowers. Parental genotypes: Parent 1 = bb (homozygous recessive, white), Parent 2 = Bb (heterozygous, colored). Assume random gamete formation and equal probability of each gamete. What is the probability that an offspring will show the recessive white phenotype?
solution: Parent1 gametes: only b. Parent2 gametes: B (1/2) or b (1/2). Offspring genotypes: b×B -> Bb (colored), b×b -> bb (white). Probability white = P(parent2 supplies b) = 1/2 = 50%.

prompt: One gene controls flower color with two alleles: R and W. Genotype-to-phenotype mapping: RR = red flowers, RW = pink flowers (intermediate phenotype), WW = white flowers. Each parent contributes one allele to offspring; gametes are equally likely. Both parents are phenotypically pink and thus have genotype RW. What is the probability that a randomly chosen offspring of these two parents will be pink? (Give your answer as a decimal between 0 and 1.)
solution: Each RW parent produces R or W gametes with probability 1/2. Offspring genotype probabilities from RW × RW: RR = 1/4 (R×R), RW = 1/4 (R×W), WR = 1/4 (W×R), WW = 1/4 (W×W). RW and WR both produce the pink phenotype, so probability pink = 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2 = 0.5.
rubric: Identify both parents as RW (pink) and list gamete probabilities (R or W each with 1/2).
Show offspring genotype probabilities (RR 1/4, RW 1/4, WR 1/4, WW 1/4) and combine RW + WR to get 1/2 for pink.

prompt: A human couple: mother X^R X^r (carrier), father X^R Y (unaffected). X-linked recessive allele r causes affected males (X^rY); daughters cannot be affected here. Each child's sex is independent with P(male)=P(female)=0.5; mother transmits X^r or X^R with equal probability. If the couple has three independent children, what is the probability that exactly one child is an affected male?
solution: Per child P(affected male) = P(male)*P(mother gives r) = 0.5*0.5 = 1/4. For exactly one affected male in 3 independent children: C(3,1)*(1/4)*(3/4)^2 = 3*(1/4)*(9/16) = 27/64 ≈ 0.421875.

prompt: A diploid somatic cell from a fictional insect species has 2n = 12. Normal meiosis halves the chromosome number so typical gametes have n = 6. During meiosis I, one homologous chromosome pair fails to segregate (nondisjunction), so both homologs go to the same daughter nucleus. Meiosis II then proceeds normally (sister chromatids separate) for all cells. Counting whole chromosomes in individual gametes after meiosis II, how many chromosomes will the gametes that carry the extra chromosome contain?
solution: Normal haploid n = 2n/2 = 12/2 = 6. Nondisjunction in meiosis I causes one daughter nucleus to have n+1 chromosomes and the other n-1. Thus the abnormal daughter has 6+1 = 7 whole chromosomes; meiosis II produces two gametes with 7 chromosomes each.
rubric: Identify normal haploid number n = 6 (1 point)
Apply nondisjunction in meiosis I: n+1 = 7 for gametes with the extra chromosome (1 point)

prompt: Given a single parental DNA template strand oriented 3′ to 5′ left-to-right: 3′-ATGCCATGTAAC-5′. The replication fork is moving to the right (replication machinery advances rightward along the parental strands). Use base-pairing (A↔T, C↔G) and the fact that DNA polymerase synthesizes 5′→3′ to write the full complementary newly synthesized DNA strand with 5′ and 3′ ends labeled, and state in one word whether synthesis on this template is 'leading' or 'lagging'.
solution: Template given 3′-ATGCCATGTAAC-5′. Complement bases: A→T, T→A, G→C, C→G, giving complementary sequence 5′-TACGGTACATTG-3′ (orientation reversed to 5′→3′). Because the fork and polymerase move rightward along this template so polymerase can synthesize continuously in the same direction, this is the leading strand.
rubric: Correct complementary sequence with 5′ and 3′ ends labeled (1 point)
Correct one-word label 'leading' indicating continuous synthesis (1 point)

prompt: All cells are eukaryotic somatic cells from the same species. Gene Z is single-copy nuclear; steady-state pre-mRNA production (transcription initiation events per unit time) in a specific tissue is measured. 5'→3' architecture: enhancer (~1000 bp upstream with activator site), silencer (~200 bp upstream), core promoter with a TATA box centered ~30 bp upstream of the TSS (basal machinery including TBP and Pol II must bind here to form the preinitiation complex), 5' UTR, start codon (AUG) at +50, coding exon, intron with canonical splice acceptor, remaining exons. Baseline (no mutations): high transcription initiation. Which single-nucleotide mutation would most strongly reduce Gene Z's transcription initiation rate (pre-mRNA production) in this tissue?

choices.A: A single-nucleotide mutation that disrupts the TATA box within the core promoter, preventing binding of TBP (TATA-binding protein).
choices.B: A single-nucleotide mutation in the enhancer activator-binding site that lowers the activator’s binding affinity by ~20%.
choices.C: A single-nucleotide mutation that changes the start codon (AUG → ACG) in the first coding exon.
choices.D: A single-nucleotide mutation at the intron splice acceptor site, causing aberrant splicing of the pre-mRNA.

solution: Disrupting the TATA box prevents TBP and the basal transcription machinery from forming a stable preinitiation complex at the core promoter, markedly reducing or abolishing transcription initiation (pre-mRNA production). A ~20% drop in enhancer activator binding only partially lowers activation while basal promoter-driven initiation can still occur. Changing the start codon affects translation, not initiation rate. A splice acceptor mutation impairs post‑transcriptional processing (splicing) but does not primarily reduce transcription initiation.

prompt: Start with one double-stranded circular plasmid (3000 bp). Polymerase single-base substitution error rate = 2.0e-6 errors per base per newly synthesized strand. PCR is ideal and doubles ds molecules each cycle. Number of PCR cycles = 5. Count all newly synthesized single strands over the 5 cycles (original two strands are not counted). What is the expected total number of single-base substitutions introduced during the 5 PCR cycles? Give a numeric expectation (may be fractional).
solution: After 5 cycles: number of double-stranded molecules = 2^5 = 32. Total single strands = 2 * 32 = 64. Newly synthesized single strands = 64 - 2 (original) = 62. Each new strand has 3000 bp, so total newly synthesized bases = 62 * 3000 = 186000. Expected substitutions = 186000 * 2.0e-6 = 0.372.
rubric: Compute total strands and newly synthesized strands: 64 total, 64-2 = 62 newly synthesized (0.5 point).
Multiply newly synthesized strands * 3000 bp * 2.0e-6 to get expected mutations = 0.372 (1.0 point).

prompt: Species: Lentea. Seed shape is controlled by a single autosomal locus with two alleles: S (spherical) is completely dominant to s (elongated). Both parents are heterozygous (Ss × Ss). Assuming Mendelian segregation and random union of gametes, what is the probability that a single offspring will display the spherical seed phenotype?
solution: Each parent produces gametes S and s at 1/2 each. Offspring genotypes from Ss × Ss: 1/4 SS, 1/2 Ss, 1/4 ss. Spherical phenotype = SS or Ss = 1/4 + 1/2 = 3/4 = 75%.

prompt: Alleles/genotypes unknown; only transmission pattern is given. Pedigree summary: Family A: Mother M (affected) and Father F1 (unaffected) have three children: Child1 (male, affected), Child2 (female, affected), Child3 (female, affected). Family B: Father F2 (affected) and Mother N (unaffected) have two children: Child4 (male, unaffected), Child5 (female, unaffected). No evidence of sex-limited expression, lethality, or sex-chromosome linkage. Assume the trait is due to either a single cytoplasmic factor (e.g., mitochondrial) or a single nuclear gene. Which inheritance model best fits these transmission facts?
solution: Affected mother M transmits the trait to all her children of both sexes, while affected father F2 transmits to none. This pattern matches mitochondrial (strictly maternal) inheritance, where mothers pass to all offspring and fathers do not transmit. Autosomal dominant/recessive and X-linked dominant do not predict both observations simultaneously (e.g., an affected father in X-linked dominant would transmit to all daughters).

prompt: Humans: males = XY, females = XX. Alleles on X: Xr = trait, X+ = normal. Trait is X-linked recessive (males XrY show phenotype; females only if XrXr). Pedigree facts: I-1 (male) unaffected × I-2 (female) carrier (X+ Xr) produce II-1 (male) affected, II-2 (female) unaffected carrier, II-3 (male) unaffected. II-1 (affected male) × unrelated non-carrier female produce III-1 (male) unaffected and III-2 (female) unaffected carrier (inherited Xr from father). II-2 (carrier) × unaffected male II-4 produce III-3 (male) affected and III-4 (female) unaffected. Assume no new mutations. Based on these pedigree facts, which feature best supports X-linked recessive inheritance for this trait?

choices.A: Affected fathers frequently transmit the trait to their sons.
choices.B: Affected individuals appear equally often in males and females across generations.
choices.C: More males are affected than females, trait passes through carrier females, and affected fathers do not pass the trait to their sons.
choices.D: Every affected parent has at least one affected child regardless of sex.

solution: X-linked recessive predicts higher male incidence because males are hemizygous; affected males cannot pass their X (Xr) to sons (they pass Y) but can pass Xr to daughters (who become carriers if father is XrY and mother contributes X+). The pedigree shows multiple affected males (II-1, III-3), carrier mothers producing affected sons (II-2 → III-3), and an affected father producing a carrier daughter and an unaffected son (II-1 → III-2 and III-1). These observations match C and rule out A, B, D.
